newsitem.title: FRANCE: Luxury goods giant LVMH profit falls on Guinness sale.
newsitem.headline: Luxury goods giant LVMH profit falls on Guinness sale.

text.p: Luxury goods giant LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton said on Thursday its profits fell in 1996 after a loss on the sale of shares in British drinks group Guinness Plc .
LVMH sold a third of its Guinness stock to help pay for a $2.6 billion purchase of 61.25 percent of U.S. prestige retail chain Duty Free Shoppers (DFS).

Net attributable profit fell to 3.68 billion francs ($647.2 million) from 4.05 billion in 1995 after the company took a 615 million franc charge due mainly to the capital loss on the Guinness sale, LVMH said.

Profit excluding exceptional items rose six percent to 4.3 billion francs, helped by a five percent rise in sales, sharply reduced financial expenses and higher returns on its holding in Guinness, which was 14 percent at the end of the year.

LVMH's stock initally fell on the results but recovered after Chairman Bernard Arnault said the company would amortise the DFS stake over 40 years, and not over 25 to 30 as previously envisaged. A spokeswoman said this meant the goodwill amortisation would weigh less on annual results.
Arnault said LVMH suspended its efforts to buy out DFS minority shareholder Robert Miller after talks became difficult, but he did not rule out an eventual deal.
Miller said on Wednesday that LVMH reneged on an agreement in principle to buy his stake and he expected to take legal action.

LVMH has also been challenged in court over its other recent acquisition, the Chateau d'Yquem vineyard which makes Sauterne wines. Manager and minority owner Count Alexandre de Lur-Saluces contests a deal by other family members to sell 55 percent.

"I wrote to him and asked him to stay on (as manager), but he has refused several times to see me," Arnault said. LVMH had repeatedly assured Lur-Saluces that the group would not cheapen the wine-making process to wring more profits from the property, he said.

LVMH, whose products span the range of French luxury goods from Moet Chandon champagnes to Louis Vuitton designer luggage and Christian Dior perfumes, reported a four percent drop in operating profit to 7.02 billion francs from 7.29 billion.

It said the drop was partly due to lower sales and profits on perfumes and beauty products following LVMH's campaign to block sales to parallel channels that supply discounters, tarnishing the image of its Christian Dior and other perfumes.
Officials said they expected the sector to recover in 1997.

Sales and profits also fell at the cognac and spirits division, reflecting shrunken corporate entertainment budgets in Japan. The yen's fall against the franc further weighed on the division's results.
LVMH said gains in the dollar and pound would partly offset the impact of the yen's weakness this year, and it has also hedged some of its yen currency risk.
The champagne division improved in 1996 while designer luggage, its largest division, reported a jump in operating profit to 3.9 billion francs from 3.5 billion.

Arnault said the group aimed to increase sales and profits this year. He reiterated that DFS would have a positive impact on LVMH's cashflow and pre-exceptional profit before goodwill amortisation, and would increase operating profit by 30 percent.

Miller's presence as a significant minority shareholder would not affect the DFS development strategy which Arnault said was already in place. The strategy was based on opening new shops, at a pace of roughly 10 a year, and penetrating emerging Asian markets.
LVMH's stock was up 1.15 percent at 1,325 francs at 1330 GMT. ($ = 5.686 French Francs)
